strengths: Addresses a genuine and important practical limitation of existing image immunization methods (PhotoGuard, DAYN): per-image optimization is too slow and memory-heavy for large-scale deployment. The idea of learning a universal 'immunizer' network inspired by universal adversarial networks is sensible and, to the authors' knowledge, new in this specific setting.
First extension of image immunization to video content, an area previously infeasible due to computational cost, with a demonstrated runtime reduction from ~64 hours to under a second on their setup.

Reasonably broad evaluation protocol: comparisons against PhotoGuard-E/D and random noise, multiple metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, SSIM (Noise), CLIP-T), a 67-participant user study, loss-term and loss-weight ablations, and counter-attack robustness (JPEG compression, CNN denoiser) — an aspect many prior defenses fail.

Honest limitations section acknowledging per-editing-tool retraining requirements; supplementary material includes additional qualitative results with InstructPix2Pix, non-human objects, and prompt-agnosticism experiments.
Clear and well-organized presentation, with a standardized test protocol (seen/unseen splits, curated prompts) that could benefit future work.
weaknesses: The core method is conceptually simple — a UNet++ producing masked perturbations, trained end-to-end through the diffusion editing model. The main 'editing failure' loss (Eq. 3) minimizes the L1 magnitude of the edited output in the unmasked region, i.e., it drives the edited background toward zero magnitude (a black/gray background). This is a crude proxy for 'editing failure' and does not directly enforce preservation of the subject or semantic prompt misalignment; it risks degenerate solutions and its generalization to editing models/loss landscapes not seen in training is unclear.

The quantitative margins over PhotoGuard-D in editing failure are small and mixed: on unseen data, PG-D actually achieves a better (lower) SSIM (0.523 vs. 0.534), and differences on other metrics are modest, yet the paper repeatedly claims 'superior results' and 'substantial degradation' of edits. Claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence.
DAYN is claimed to be inferior in robustness (Table 1), but is never compared quantitatively because it is not open source; the quantitative comparison is limited to PhotoGuard variants only.

Evaluation scale is limited: 1,000 images from a single dataset (CCP) of humans only, only 75 seen and 75 unseen test images, and only 4 videos for the headline video contribution; no statistical significance testing, no varying diffusion samplers/timestep counts, and only two counter-attack types.

The method is white-box and per-tool: the immunizer must be retrained against each specific editing model, and generalization to unseen editing models is shown only qualitatively (InstructPix2Pix). Against adaptive adversaries using other editing models or stronger purification attacks, protection may not hold.

Training details (22 hours on an A100, 350 epochs, batch size 5) mean the approach trades per-image cost for a substantial upfront training cost per editing tool; the practical cost-benefit for users who edit with changing/updated models (e.g., new fine-tuned SD versions) is not analyzed.

Prompt-agnosticity is claimed based on PhotoGuard's findings and a small supplementary experiment with a single training image; the training prompts were generated by ChatGPT for background editing, so diversity of editing intent is limited.

strengths: The core motivation is compelling and practical: existing immunization methods (PhotoGuard, DAYN) require per-image optimization, and a learned immunizer that runs in a single forward pass (0.07s vs. 911s) with 250,000x speedup addresses a genuine scalability bottleneck for real-world deployment.

The end-to-end training framework (Algorithm 1) connecting a learned immunizer with the editing model through backpropagation is clearly described, and the ablation study (Table 4) properly isolates the contribution of each loss term.

The evaluation includes multiple complementary aspects: quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, CLIP-T), a user study with 67 participants, ablations on the loss weight, counter-attack robustness (denoiser, JPEG), and qualitative results extending to video, non-human objects, and a second editing tool (InstructPix2Pix).
Extension of immunization to video content, while modest in scale, is a new capability in this line of work.
The paper is generally well written and easy to follow, and code availability improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially an application of universal adversarial networks (UANs, [19,41]) to the immunization domain, as the authors themselves acknowledge. The main contribution is the new application and training recipe rather than a fundamentally new technique, and the technical machinery (UNet++ noise generator + adversarial loss against a frozen editing model) is straightforward.

The Ledit objective (Eq. 3) is degenerate and potentially trivially gameable: it minimizes the L1 magnitude of the edited output in the unmasked region, effectively pushing edited backgrounds toward a flat/zero background (visible as gray/destructive outputs in Figs. 1, 3, 4, and 9). It is unclear that this reflects meaningful disruption of the editing process rather than simply destroying the output, and the paper does not analyze whether a simpler objective (or even simpler perturbations) could achieve similar results. Random Noise already achieves SSIM 0.586 vs. DiffVax's 0.519, a narrow margin.

Claims of superiority are not fully supported by the results: on unseen data, PhotoGuard-D achieves better SSIM (0.523 vs. 0.534) and comparable PSNR, and no statistical significance testing is reported for the small differences across methods. The claim of being 'the fastest, most cost-effective, and robust method available' is overreaching.

Missing baseline: no quantitative comparison with DAYN [33] (CVPR 2024), the most direct competitor; Table 1 dismisses it as not open-source, but reimplementing or obtaining it appears feasible, and the paper's strong comparative claims are weakened without it.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only 75 test images per split, a single primary editing model (SD v1.5 inpainting), background-editing prompts only, and a video evaluation on just 4 videos. InstructPix2Pix results are qualitative only with no quantitative support.

No adaptive attacker evaluation: robustness is tested only against a fixed denoiser and JPEG compression. An adaptive adversary aware of the defense (e.g., alternative samplers, DDIM inversion, stronger purification, or editing models not seen during training) is not considered, despite adversarial robustness being a central claimed contribution. Table 1's 'Robustness Against Attacks' check is thus largely unsupported.

Internal inconsistency in the narrative: the paper claims the framework is 'adaptable to any diffusion-based editing method' and 'universal,' yet the limitations section concedes it requires separate retraining per editing tool (22 hours each), and Table 1 marks previous methods as non-scalable while the training itself is costly and per-tool.

Key implementation details affecting soundness are unclear: the number of diffusion timesteps used when differentiating through SD(·) in the Ledit loss, how gradients flow through the multi-step sampling chain, and the perturbation budget kappa actually enforced are not specified.

Presentation issues: minor but noticeable sloppiness (e.g., 'N\A' in Table 3, missing punctuation in the introduction, inconsistent claim wording), and the seen/unseen split conflates image and prompt novelty in ways that complicate interpretation of generalization.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing diffusion-editing immunization methods (PhotoGuard, DAYN) require per-image optimization, making them impractical at scale; DiffVax's learned 'immunizer' (inspired by universal adversarial networks) is a natural and sensible solution, and the paper is, to my knowledge, the first optimization-free immunization framework for diffusion-based editing.

Impressive practical gains: single-forward-pass immunization (0.07s/image vs. ~207–912s for PhotoGuard), reduced GPU memory (5.6GB vs. 9.5–15GB), and a first extension to video immunization (64 hours to under a second), all clearly quantified.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation for a defense paper: quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, CLIP-T), a 67-participant human study on Prolific, ablations of both loss terms, hyperparameter (alpha) sensitivity analysis, counter-attack robustness (denoiser, JPEG), and qualitative results on unseen images, non-human objects, and a second editing tool (InstructPix2Pix).
Prompt-agnostic design is empirically supported with a dedicated experiment (supplementary S.3), and the two-term loss design is well justified by the ablation study.
The paper contributes a standardized benchmark protocol (seen/unseen splits with diverse prompts), which is valuable for this emerging area, and promises open-source code.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: only 75 seen and 75 unseen test images drawn from a 1,000-image CCP training set, and the video evaluation uses only 4 videos with 4 prompts each. These small test sets make the central generalization claims fragile, and no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported.

Comparison with DAYN is mostly rhetorical (Table 1 claims, closed-source), so the claimed superiority over the closest prior work is not quantitatively verified; the strongest quantitative baseline is only PhotoGuard-D, against which some margins (e.g., unseen SSIM 0.534 vs. 0.523) are modest.

Counter-attack robustness is evaluated against only two relatively weak attacks (an off-the-shelf CNN denoiser and JPEG compression); stronger purification attacks (e.g., diffusion-based purification, more aggressive compression, adversarial fine-tuning) are untested, so claims of robustness may be stronger than the evidence.

The method is per-editing-tool (trained against SD v1.5 inpainting); transferability is shown only qualitatively for InstructPix2Pix, and the framework also assumes access to an accurate mask of the target region (via SAM), which is a notable practical assumption not fully discussed.

Ethical/dual-use considerations are underdeveloped: the paper displays immunized images of identifiable real individuals (e.g., well-known researchers) and discusses protective uses, but does not discuss potential misuse of the immunization technique itself or IRB/consent considerations for the human study and image datasets.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'fulfills all criteria for an ideal model,' 'universal tool,' and the 250,000x speedup headline, which is computed against the least favorable comparison; limitations section acknowledges the per-tool limitation but the abstract/introduction do not fully temper these claims.
